fix.sql:
ALTER SYSTEM SET wal_compression = on;  -- lz4 or zstd on PostgreSQL 15+
SELECT pg_reload_conf();
fix.summary: Touch each page once per checkpoint: batch the changes (one statement for many rows, sorted by key) rather than many scattered single-row writes. Every index on the table adds its own WAL: drop indexes nobody reads (see Indexes). When full-page images dominate, wal_compression shrinks them, and a longer checkpoint interval logs fewer of them.

About 86% of it is full-page images: the first change to each page after a checkpoint logs the whole 8 KB page.

verify: Re-scan: its share of the WAL and the bytes per row should drop.

fix.summary: Leave room on each page so updated rows fit next to the old version: a fillfactor of 85–90 is typical for tables updated often. It applies to pages written from now on; existing pages get the room as rows move (pg_repack rewrites the table online if you want it at once). If an index covers a column that changes on every update (updated_at, status, counters), dropping it makes those updates HOT too.

findings.summary: An update that changes no indexed column and finds room on the same page is HOT: it writes no index entries and its old version is cleaned up without VACUUM. None of wide's 21K updates were, so each wrote a new entry in both of its indexes. 100% of them moved to another page because their own was full (fillfactor 100).
